result:
There is a specific shade of blue that only exists for about twenty minutes a day. Photographers call it the "blue hour"—that quiet pocket of time just after the sun has dipped below the horizon, before the true dark of night settles in. The streetlights flicker on, glowing amber against a cobalt sky, and the world seems to hold its breath. Everything is neither one thing nor the other. It isn’t day, and it isn’t night. 

I find myself endlessly fascinated by the spaces in between.

We spend so much of our energy focused on beginnings and endings. We celebrate the launch of a project and its completion; we mark the departure time and the arrival time; we remember the day we met someone and, sometimes, the day we said goodbye. Our stories are built around milestones—solid, definable points on a map. 

Yet, most of existence actually happens in the hallway between those rooms. 

Think about an airport terminal at 4:00 AM. It is a fundamentally strange place, suspended outside of normal geography and time. Someone in a business suit is drinking an espresso next to someone in pajamas eating a slice of pizza, and nobody blinks an eye. Nobody *lives* in the terminal; everyone is purely in transit, shed of their usual context, existing entirely between who they were in the city they left and who they need to be in the city they are flying toward. There is a weird, quiet freedom in that suspension. Because you aren't anywhere yet, nothing is expected of you except to wait.

Nature loves these thresholds, too. An estuary—where the freshwater of a river meets the saltwater of the tide—is one of the most vibrant, life-sustaining ecosystems on Earth precisely because it refuses to be just a river or just an ocean. Autumn isn't just the death of summer or the prologue to winter; it’s a riot of color triggered entirely by the act of letting go. 

Even meaning itself relies on the gaps. Claude Debussy once remarked that music is the space between the notes. Without the rests, a symphony would just be an overwhelming wall of noise. Look at the very screen you are reading right now: if you removed all the blank spaces between these words, this entire reflection would collapse into an unreadable block of characters. The emptiness isn't a lack of something; it is the exact architecture that allows the words to make sense.

It is easy to resent transitions in our own lives. Waiting for news, learning a skill we aren't good at yet, healing from a loss, standing at a crossroads without a clear sign—these moments feel restless and uncomfortable. We want clarity. We want to arrive. 

Whenever that impatience creeps in, it might be worth remembering the blue hour. A transition isn't wasted time, and a threshold isn't a void. Sometimes, the most honest, transformative place to be is mid-step, suspended between the exhale and the next breath, watching the streetlights come on.
